lines.note: Fôbucu is hōbuku, religious or ceremonial clothing; the Portuguese explicitly identifies the wearers as Buddhist religious. The damaged b was read as t by OCR. Bõzos is an embedded upright word, with a full stop following it in this impression.

runs.text: veſtidos de que vſão em ſeus officios, & ſo-

lines.note: This continues the definition, specifying clothes worn in religious offices and solemnities. Officios refers to observances here, not simply occupations; the last so- belongs to solennidades on the next line.
Lennidades completes solennidades, solemn celebrations. The narrow letter after nn is i, not the OCR u; this is a continuation, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Bolſo da vela quãdo vai cõ vẽto.

lines.note: Fobucuro is hobukuro, the belly or pocket formed by a wind-filled sail. Bolso da vela and quãdo vai cõ vẽto give that nautical context; the abbreviated quãdo has a worn nasal mark, not the OCR quido.
Fǒca is hōka, a conjurer or performer. Fǒcauo suru means performing such tricks; the Portuguese action begins with Fa- and continues on the next line.

runs.text: zer officio, ou obras de trejeitador enganando

lines.note: Fazer officio, ou obras de trejeitador describes acting as a conjurer and deceiving the viewer. The scan supports officio, including its faint i, rather than offcio.

A vista artificiosamente completes the thought: deceiving sight by artifice. The damaged middle letters still support artificioſamente, not artificinſamente; vista's short s is left as printed/OCR-read.
Foca is hoka, outside or other; cono foca is kono hoka, beyond this or in addition. Portuguese Fora and Alem di- separate the spatial and additive uses.
Isto finishes the preceding Portuguese phrase. Iyeno foca is ie no hoka, outside the house, exactly matching Fora da casa; the old romanization is not modernized.

runs.text: Sono focano guiuo nochi catari mara-

lines.note: Sono focano giu means the remaining matter; nochi catari introduces telling it later. Mara- belongs to the historical polite ending continued below, not to an independent word.

Xǒzu completes the historical polite/future expression, rendered in Portuguese as discussing the rest later. Cu at the end starts Cugue across the line break; it is not a one-syllable standalone example.

runs.text: gue buquano fitobito yori focaua qiogiù

lines.note: Cugue buqua names court nobles and the warrior class; yori foca ua means apart from them. Qiogiù is the printed form for residence in the capital in this quotation; its faint one-sided accent is retained rather than regularized from pronunciation.

Ni fito aritomo miyezariqeri completes the negative account of people being present. The citation is provisionally Taif., the usual Taiheiki label, with its final f severely worn; the surviving area after i and the book citation support it, but this is not a cleanly preserved letter.

runs.text: Tirando os nobres aßi Cũgues co-

lines.note: Livro 30 identifies the cited book. Tirando os nobres means excepting the nobles; Cũgues is embedded Japanese court terminology but looks italic in this line, so it is not automatically made upright.

runs.text: mo caualeiros não auia dentro do

lines.note: The Portuguese finishes by saying there were no people within Miyaco except the named noble groups. Miyaco is printed upright within the italic explanation; nao auia retains the historical spelling of modern não havia.
Focafoca is an adverb explained here as impetuously or forcefully, not limited to the modern warm/fluffy sense of hokahoka. Impetuoſamente is supported by the scan and the following ou com força.
Focafocato tçuqi touoſu is hokahoka to tsuki tōsu, piercing forcefully through something. The Portuguese com força belongs to the preceding definition; Vt introduces this example.

runs.text: Modo de traſpaßar com adaga, ou lança furio

lines.note: The example is explained as driving a dagger or spear through furiously. Furio continues into samente below without an added editorial hyphen; traſpaßar retains the OCR ligature distinction.
Samente completes furiosamente. Item then introduces another sense, inconsiderately, rather than another Japanese headword.
Focafocato monouo yû means speaking heedlessly. The Portuguese Falar algũa begins the corresponding definition; the source's nasal mark is kept on u.
Cousa desatentadamente completes speaking something heedlessly. The first consonant is a worn d, and the apparent gap inside desatentadamente is mostly a damaged a, not good evidence for two words.

runs.text: Forte, cerca, ou tranqueira q̃ ſe

lines.note: Focagamaye is hokagamae, outer works or an outer enclosure. Forte, cerca, tranqueira are alternative descriptions of a defensive perimeter, consistent with hoka plus kamae.

runs.text: faz fora da fortaleza, ou da cidade, pouoa-

lines.note: The enclosure is built outside a fortress, city, or settlement. Pouoa- is continued below; the line does not introduce another example.
Ção completes pouoação, settlement. The short physical line is a real continuation and is kept with its own stable ID and readable crop.

runs.text: Vela que aparece ao longe. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Focague is hokage in the sail sense, a sail visible at a distance. The following Item adds a related meaning; it should not be interpreted as the modern firelight homophone just from kana.
Sombra da vela gives the second meaning, the shadow or silhouette of a sail. This confirms the nautical reading of the preceding headword.
Fôcai is hōkai, equated with xecai, sekai, the world. The printed circumflex is distinct from the unaccented Focai in the next entry.
Focai is hokai, a portable food container. Caxa is the historical spelling of caixa, not cara; Bentò is an upright embedded Japanese comparator, retaining the printed grave accent.

runs.text: leua por caminho, ou na embarcação com co-

lines.note: The container is carried on a journey or aboard a vessel. Com co- begins com comer dentro, with food inside, continued below.
Mer dentro completes the explanation of the container's contents. Comer functions nominally as food here, not an instruction to eat indoors.

Fǒcan is an honorific term for a letter, glossed with fragrant writing and fumi. Cobaxij fude is severely worn at its beginning; although kōbashii is the expected sense, no dependable accent survives over o, so the unaccented spelling is retained.

Carta falando com reverencia da pessoa explains the honorific use of the preceding Japanese expression. It is about deferential reference to someone's letter, not a separate sense of fude as a physical brush.
Focani is hoka ni, outside or outward, marked Adu. The Portuguese distinction Fora / pera fora expresses location versus direction without requiring a change to the Japanese spelling.
Focaqebune is hokakebune, a sailing vessel. The scan and Embarcação que vai à vela agree; qe belongs to ke, while bune is the voiced form of fune.
Foccai is hokkai, the northern sea, explicitly unpacked as qita no umi. The doubled c represents the consonant sequence, not a missing vowel.
Fôcǒ denotes covering or muffling the face, rebuço. Fôcǒ suru is the corresponding action; the two different o accents are retained as visible rather than collapsed in the transcription.
Por rebuço no rosto completes putting a covering over the face. The spelling roſto is left to the OCR's typographic reading, rather than inferred from a general s-before-t rule.
Foccocu is hokkoku, northern provinces or countries, glossed qita no cuni. The explanation continues below and supports the doubled consonant.
Do Norte completes the geographical definition. This short line has its own body rectangle; it is neither a heading nor page furniture.
Foccu is hokku, the opening verse; iydaſu fajimeno cu explicitly describes the first verse brought forth. The nasal mark over the final e in ſẽ is visible and belongs to sentença across the break.

runs.text: ou verſos que ſe enfião, & cõ

lines.note: Vtas refers to Japanese poems and is upright in the Portuguese explanation. Enfião means the verses are strung together; the worn nasal ending is not the OCR enfido, and cõ starts continuão below.
Tinuão tè cento completes continuing the linked verses up to one hundred. The damaged u is supported by the remaining strokes and cõ above; the printed historical tè is preserved.
Fochifochito is an expressive adverb, first explained through small objects falling. The Portuguese cou- continues into cousas, not a Japanese fragment.

runs.text: ſas miudas, ou modo de ſoar algũa couſa que ſe

lines.note: The definition also covers the sound of something breaking. Algũa is retained with its tilde over u; nothing in the sense licenses relocating that mark.
Fochifochito mameuo tçumu illustrates eating beans with a crunching sound. The final tçu- continues to mu; the faint terminal stroke is retained without introducing a new hyphen elsewhere.

runs.text: Comer grãos que ſoão entre os dentes

lines.note: Mu completes the Japanese verb. The Portuguese explains grains sounding between the teeth, supporting the expressive reading rather than a silent picking action inferred from modern tsumu alone.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Modo de ler deuagar, & como ſo-

lines.note: A further use is reading slowly, as if spelling out letters. So- continues with letrando at the top of column 2; this is body text, not a catchword.

Letrando completes soletrando from column 1. Fochifochito yomu is reading slowly; the m is worn into separated strokes and was read as n, but the surviving strokes, the Portuguese, and the parallel yomu on the next line support m.
Xifoxito yomu completes the alternative foxifoxito yomu, another expressive form for reading slowly. It is a continuation of the example, not a new entry beginning with xi.
Fôchô is hōchō, identified with the phoenix Fôuǒ and glossed bird of the sun. Paßaro, not Paßuro, is the Portuguese noun; the accent mixture in Fôuǒ is retained as printed.

Fochǒ describes swelling, hōchō suru. The first o and the example are abraded; NINJAL's Fǒchǒ supports the lexical identity but does not justify supplying every missing accent in this impression. The italic S. is kept.
Fǒchǒ is hōchō, a kitchen knife or cleaver, distinct from the preceding swelling word despite similar sound. Manchil and cutelo de trinchar name the cutting tool.
The definition specifies cutting in the kitchen, then gives Fǒchǒ suru as the action. Cor- belongs to Portuguese Cortar on the next line.

runs.text: tar, ou trinchar com eſte inſtrumento.

lines.note: Tar completes Cortar, followed by carving with this instrument. The long-s form in instrumento is preserved, not replaced on modern typographic grounds.

runs.text: O que corta, ou trincha bem com eſ-

lines.note: Fochǒjin is the person skilled in carving with the knife. The initial vowel is too worn to supply the accent solely from the related Fǒchǒ entry; the current spelling preserves that limitation.
Ta completes esta faca, this knife or cleaver. This describes the practitioner's skill and closes the preceding entry.

Fôco is hōko, treasure storehouse, explicitly tacara no cura. Gudão is retained as the printed warehouse word, with logea offering a parallel Portuguese explanation rather than grounds to modernize it.
Fazenda ou fato explains the goods stored in the warehouse. Fato here is belongings or goods, not the modern English-looking sense of fact.

This Fôco is a precious vessel, tacara no tçubo. The Portuguese is provisionally Bojão, a jar: most of j is worn but its low stroke survives; Borão was an OCR misreading, and the context specifically calls for a vessel.
Estima completes de preço, ou estima, of value or esteem. This belongs to the precious jar, not the warehouse sense above.
Focǒ is hokō, walking, paraphrased ayumi yuqu. Fo- starts the same word in an example continued on the following line.
Cǒ suru completes Focǒ suru, to walk. Idem refers back to Ir, ou andar; there is no new headword cǒ.
Fôcô is hōkō, service. The two circumflexes distinguish this printed form from Focǒ, walking; the short definition is complete on this line.

runs.text: Hũa laya de lança. ¶ Item, Fiſ-

lines.note: Foco is hoko, a spear, with a second sense beginning Fiſ-. The vowel is short in the transcription, unlike the several hō- compounds nearby.
Ga completes fisga, a fishing spear, specifying fishermen's use. The line is a continuation of the second sense of hoko.
Fǒco is a drum, literally idaqu tçuzzumi, a drum one holds. The definition identifies a military use, so this should not be merged with the spear entry.

runs.text: na guerra da China, & doutros reinos.

lines.note: The drum is said to be used in Chinese warfare and other kingdoms. This is the geographical continuation of the preceding definition, not an embedded Japanese example.

runs.text: Eſteira q̃ poem de baixo do gauião,

lines.note: Focodare is hokodare, the mat beneath a hawk or falcon on its perch. Esteira and the bird terminology support the falconry sense rather than a spear attachment inferred from hoko alone.
Sobre hum pao completes the description of the bird's perch. The right rule is visible beyond the punctuation, allowing the short line to be checked without guessing its end.
Fôcôdate concerns showing one's service or merit. The following Fôcô is entirely upright Japanese, including F, which OCR had accidentally attached to the preceding italic span.
Dateuo suru fitogia completes hōkōdate o suru hito ja, a person who makes a display of service. The damaged vowel is e, consistent with the headword and surviving strokes, rather than datauo.

runs.text: moſtrar no ſeruiço do ſenhor diligente, ou be-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes seeking to appear diligent in the lord's service or deserving of reward. Senhor has a worn o, not the OCR senher; be- continues to benemerito.
Nemerito completes benemerito, well-deserving. This small continuation must remain body text even though its content is only part of a word.

runs.text: Homem que ſerue a algum ſenhor,

lines.note: Fôcônin is hōkōnin, a person serving a lord. The printed comma after senhor connects to the income clause below, rather than the OCR full stop.
The servant receives renda or tença, income or a stipend, from that lord. This narrows the definition beyond any person doing a service.

Focore, ruru, eta gives forms of hokoreru, coming unsewn or apart, explicitly equated with Focoroburu. The second form is ruru: the abraded u and NINJAL's headword record support correcting OCR raru, without changing the printed Focore stem.
The clothing comes unstitched by itself. X. is an upright register abbreviation; its period belongs to the same upright label, not an isolated italic run.

Focori is hokori, dust; focori ga tatçu means dust rises. Several strokes in Focoriga are worn, but the remaining ri and ga plus the repeated headword support that reading. Portuguese Pò / pò has a grave-like mark in both places, not an editorially supplied circumflex.
This Focori is the verb hokoru, to boast or become proud, with forms ru and otta. It is a separate entry from dust even though the romanized stem is identical.

Narichicaqiǒua chôuǒni names Narichika-kyō and favour or patronage in the cited example. The weak mark in chôuǒ is retained; the following Portuguese confirms the favour of the ruler, not a new lexical definition here.

runs.text: Feiq. Lib. i. Eſte homem aleuan-

lines.note: Focori completes the quotation's action, becoming proud through royal favour. Feiq. identifies the Heike citation, followed by Lib. i; the label appears italic here and is kept switchable rather than automatically forced upright.

runs.text: tandoſe com as merces do Rei. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese describes exalting oneself through the king's favours. Man- begins another Japanese example, continued with qini below, not a Portuguese word.
Manqini focoru completes manki ni hokoru, becoming conceited or proud. Enſoberbecerſe is the Portuguese equivalence and closes the verb's examples.

Focorobi, uru, ita gives hokorobiru, something coming unsewn by itself. The printed u-ending is the dictionary's inflectional notation, not an invitation to replace the historical verb with a modern spelling.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Nos poetas ſe uſa por abrir a ro-

lines.note: A poetic use follows: a rose or similar flower opening. This connects seams opening with blossoms opening; it is not an unrelated headword inferred from Nos poetas.
Sa completes rosa and closes the poetic sense. The short continuation is preserved as a physical line, with enough crop context to identify it.
Focorobi is the noun for an opening seam or unstitched place. Focorobiuo begins the example of sewing it up, with the verb on the next line.
Nǔ is nū, to sew, fitting Coſer o que eſta deſcoſido. The first n has separated worn strokes that OCR turned into ni; no independent i is needed or supported between n and the accented u.

runs.text: Ponta do dardo, ou lança. Item,

lines.note: Focoſaqi is hokosaki, the point of a spear or dart. The long s is left as the scan/OCR reading, not reduced to match a normalized headword list.
The second meaning is the point of a fishing spear. Fisga refers back to the fishing implement under Foco rather than an anatomical part of a fish.

Focqe is Hokke, the Lotus teaching/text. Xaca and Foquequiǒ are upright embedded names; the latter is an irregular printed form of the Lotus Sutra title, not normalized to an expected Focqeqiǒ. Hamado lacks a clearly surviving initial c in this impression, so that apparent omission is retained and flagged.

The second sense is the sect of the Focquexus, Hokke adherents. The q's descender was misread as j; the word is upright within the Portuguese sentence, and its irregular spelling is preserved rather than replaced with a modern sect name.

runs.text: Certa laya de peças delgadas da

lines.note: Focqen identifies a kind of thin Chinese fabric or piece goods. The Portuguese peças is about cloth here; the broad crop includes the start of China below but does not omit this line's right edge.
China completes the origin of the cloth. It is a genuine final body line; the separate Focqet below is the page catchword and is not duplicated here.
